source.title: Mechanistic Unlearning: Robust Knowledge Unlearning and Editing via Mechanistic Localization
source.authors: P. Guo; Aaquib Syed; A. Sheshadri; Aidan Ewart; G. Dziugaite

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests localized factual editing/unlearning against alternative prompting, relearning, and latent-knowledge probes. Its results refine the broad claim: output-tracing methods are vulnerable in some settings, while fact-lookup localization is more robust, though not immune to recovery.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on factual editing/unlearning and on attacks against edited facts. It does not test quantization or ablation of a single activation direction. Standard edited-answer metrics and detailed mask-sweep plots are not included as recovery rows where they do not measure recovery of the original knowledge.
record.test_reason: The study checks whether the original answer comes back after localized fine-tuning edits and unlearning. It uses four attacks: MCQ prompting, soft prompts, relearning on half the forget set, and linear probes. Output-tracing (OT) localizations prove shallow on several of these. The proposed fact-lookup (FLU) localization is more robust but not immune. Most tasks are editing (injecting a false answer). Only Sports-Unlearning (Appendix A.1) is unlearning proper.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that localizing edits and unlearning to fact-lookup MLPs is more robust to MCQ reformatting and relearning than OT localizations and baselines. They add that FLU leaves less latent knowledge and has fewer side effects. They argue that OT methods mainly alter extraction mechanisms and leave the facts in the latent stream. The claims are made mostly for editing tasks; unlearning appears in one appendix table.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses mechanistically localized gradient fine-tuning of fact-lookup MLPs, with forget/edit, retain, and SFT losses; it does not reproduce gradient-ascent unlearning, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or quantization.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by localization and task. FLU is more robust than OT under sports MCQ prompting and relearning; Gemma-2-9B OT localizations recover over 60% under soft prompts while FLU is grouped below 40%. CounterFact relearning is weak across localizations.
record.problems: Several robustness results are presented only in figures, often averaged across models. The Sports-Unlearning table does not state its model or an unmodified-model reference for retain accuracy and MMLU. CounterFact relearning is acknowledged to be too weak as an evaluation. The probe results are indirect evidence about latent representations, not proof of deletion or a test of activation-direction ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed standard-prompt edit metrics and weight-mask sweeps are omitted where they assess the edited target or mask size rather than recovery of the original answer (Sections 3.1 and 3.4; Appendices A.4 and A.7.1). Full-Sports-Editing's 100% regained edit accuracy after relearning is omitted because the authors say the facts are not independent and that this is not a valid relearning evaluation (Appendix A.7.3, Figure 35).

untested.parts: Sports-Unlearning has no pre-edit MMLU or retain reference. Its only attack is MCQ (Table 1, A.4.1); relearning and soft prompts are run only on editing tasks. No standard unlearning benchmark (WMDP, Harry Potter) is used.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data is not tested. The only split is training on half the forgotten facts and testing on the held-out half.
Activation-direction ablation is not tested. The evidence is probes and weight-mask mechanism analysis only.
Quantization is not tested at all.
Jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information are not tested. The MCQ prompt has in-context answering examples but not the forgotten information.
FLU is not tested against quantization, direction ablation, or relearning on unrelated data.

missing.what: MCQ forget error and edit accuracy for OT, Nonlocalized and other baselines in Sports-Athlete-Editing, Full-Sports-Editing and CounterFact. This is the core E evidence that reformatting recovers non-FLU edits. The text says FLU leads the others by more than 40% in MCQ edit accuracy on Sports-Athlete-Editing, but is only slightly better on Full-Sports-Editing.
Weight-mask sweeps: AP and CT reach 0 standard forget with few masked weights, but MCQ forget accuracy stays high. Only FLU generalizes to MCQ.
Relearning across all localizations: FLU is best, but Nonlocalized, All-MLPs, Random and Random-MLPs are competitive.
Per-model probes: Attribution Patching has 100% probe forget accuracy across many layers. In Gemma-2-9b, the baselines are competitive with FLU.
Mechanism weight analysis: OT and nonlocalized masks modify extraction weights proportionally more than fact-lookup weights. This is evidence that they block access rather than delete.

record.verdict_notes: Changes from the previous verdict: (1) The duplicate items for r03, r07 and r11 are merged into one item each. For rows that measure an attack, the state is read against the recovery effect (B, C, E); A and F read inversely. This matches the earlier r19, r23, r26, r31 and r36 items. r03 is absent; r07 and r11 are observed. (2) r03 is now linked to F, because the F supports label cites it and it is FLU's only absolute MCQ number. (3) r34 is reduced to E: it is an OT comparator, the same reasoning that took F off r25. (4) Missing entry 1 now lists E, F instead of E, A, since A is scoped to Sports-Unlearning only, and it notes the slight FLU edge on Full-Sports-Editing. (5) A's untested parts now say Sports-Unlearning's only attack is MCQ. (6) The r26 problem notes the unclear base of 'about 20%', and the F limits_scope reason marks the Gemma-2-9b probe point as text-only. Unchanged context: the study is mostly editing (overwriting with a false answer); only Table 1 is unlearning proper, and it names no model. Relative statements in figure-only results cannot fix absolute recovery levels. The record's ICML peer-review claim is not supported by the text (arXiv v2). Chance: four-choice MCQ 0.25; three-sport probes and soft prompts about 0.33. No instructions in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates factual unlearning/editing and attacks on it, but does not establish that the method preserves all general abilities against a pre-edit baseline in every setting.
Relearning uses half of the original forgotten facts, not unrelated or loosely related examples. CounterFact relearning is described as too weak to be a sufficient evaluation.
No activation-direction ablation is tested. Probing intermediate representations is used to assess residual factual information, not to demonstrate a specific access-blocking mechanism conclusively.
The study tests multiple-choice prompting, paraphrases, and optimized soft prompts; it does not test jailbreaks or other languages.
The proposed fact-lookup localization is tested against the prompting and relearning evaluations used in the paper, not quantization or activation-direction ablation.

The soft-prompt text adds the hedge 'or are about equal between localizations'.
